Companies intending to provide regulated crypto-asset services in the EU generally need authorisation from the competent authority in an EU member state.
Once authorised, a CASP can provide permitted services across other EU member states through the regulatory passporting framework.
Certain already-regulated financial institutions may provide crypto-asset services under specific notification requirements rather than obtaining a separate CASP authorisation.
MiCA establishes minimum permanent capital requirements based on the type of crypto-asset services provided, including €50,000 for Class 1, €125,000 for Class 2, and €150,000 for Class 3.
CASPs must maintain the required prudential safeguards, which are generally the higher of the applicable minimum permanent capital requirement and one-quarter of the preceding year's fixed overheads.
CASPs providing custody and administration services must protect customers' crypto-assets and funds.
Customer crypto-assets must be legally and operationally distinguished from the service provider's own assets.
CASPs must establish effective and transparent procedures for receiving and handling customer complaints.
CASPs must identify, prevent, manage and disclose conflicts of interest that could negatively affect customers.
MiCA requires CASPs to maintain appropriate governance and risk-management arrangements.
MiCA establishes rules against market abuse involving crypto-assets admitted to trading or for which admission to trading has been requested.
MiCA's stablecoin-related provisions concerning asset-referenced tokens and e-money tokens began applying on 30 June 2024.
Most other provisions, including the main CASP authorisation and conduct requirements, began applying on 30 December 2024.
